<details>
The PKGBUILD defines standard metadata variables (pkgname, pkgver, arch, etc.), dependencies, sources, and checksums using typical AUR syntax. All variable assignments are static or derived from other static variables (e.g., `_pkgname`, `_deb`, `_appname`) and do not involve command substitution or execution of external programs at the top level. The `source` array references a remote Debian package and a LICENSE file, both from the official Multilogin domain, which is consistent with the package's purpose. The `sha256sums` are provided and not set to 'SKIP', so integrity verification will occur later — but that has no impact on the safety of `makepkg --printsrcinfo`.

No function bodies (e.g., `prepare()`, `package()`) are executed during `makepkg --printsrcinfo`, and there are no top-level command substitutions, `curl`, `wget`, `eval`, or other potentially dangerous constructs that would execute code while sourcing the PKGBUILD. The file uses only safe, declarative packaging constructs.

Therefore, sourcing this PKGBUILD for metadata extraction poses no risk of remote code execution, data exfiltration, or unauthorized network access.
</details>

The package is extracted using `bsdtar` to obtain the application binary and associated files, which are then installed into standard system directories. All operations are transparent and follow standard AUR packaging practices for binary packages.

The source URL points to the legitimate upstream provider (`cdn-mlx-prod.multiloginapp.com`), and the checksum ensures the downloaded `.deb` file has not been tampered with. The `prepare()` and `package()` functions perform only file extraction and installation with no obfuscated commands, network calls, or suspicious scripting. The use of `sed` to modify the desktop file is limited to standard desktop entry adjustments (fixing Exec, Icon, Comment, Categories) and removal of irrelevant entries—common in AUR packaging to integrate proprietary binaries cleanly into the system.

There are no signs of malicious behavior such as data exfiltration, remote code execution, or unauthorized system modifications. While the binary is not built from source (typical for `-bin` packages), this is expected and not inherently unsafe. The package depends only on common GUI libraries, and no dangerous options or commands are used.
</details>
